nameStory: The Purple Sandpiper gets its name from the subtle purple-gray sheen that shows on its feathers in good light, especially during breeding season. While not dramatically purple like a grape, this bird has a dusky, slate-colored plumage with purplish highlights that sets it apart from its sandier-colored cousins.
description: The Purple Sandpiper is a chunky, medium-sized shorebird about the size of a robin, with dark slate-gray plumage that looks almost charcoal in poor light. Unlike most sandpipers that prefer sandy beaches, this hardy bird is perfectly at home scrambling over slippery, wave-splashed rocks along the coast. It has a slightly curved, dark bill and bright orange-yellow legs that stand out against the dark rocks where it feeds. This is one of our toughest shorebirds, built to handle the harsh conditions of rocky coastlines in winter.

idTips.label: Dark, slate-gray plumage
idTips.description: Overall very dark coloration, almost charcoal gray, that contrasts sharply with the white foam of crashing waves - much darker than any other common sandpiper

idTips.label: Bright orange-yellow legs
idTips.description: Legs are distinctly orange to yellow, creating a striking contrast against the dark body and providing good grip on wet, algae-covered rocks

idTips.label: Rocky habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on wave-washed rocks, jetties, and breakwaters rather than sandy beaches - listen for their quiet peeping calls over the crash of waves

idTips.label: Chunky, stocky build
idTips.description: Noticeably rounder and more robust than most sandpipers, with a thick body that helps it maintain balance on slippery, uneven surfaces

idTips.label: Curved, dark bill
idTips.description: Bill is slightly downturned and completely dark, perfect for probing into crevices between rocks and prying off barnacles and snails

habitat: Purple Sandpipers are found exclusively along New England's rocky coastlines, especially on wave-splashed jetties, breakwaters, and natural rocky shores from Maine down to Massachusetts. They prefer areas where barnacles, mussels, and seaweed create rich feeding opportunities in the intertidal zone. You'll rarely see them on sandy beaches - they're specialists of the rocky coast where most other shorebirds can't get a foothold.

seasonality.spring: Small numbers may still be present in early spring before departing for Arctic breeding grounds by May. Look for slightly brighter plumage with more distinct feather edges as they molt into breeding condition.
seasonality.summer: Absent from New England during summer months as they breed in the high Arctic tundra of Canada and Alaska.
seasonality.fall: First returning birds appear in October, with numbers building through November as they arrive from their Arctic breeding grounds. Juveniles show slightly paler, more scaled plumage patterns.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for Purple Sandpipers - they're most numerous and easiest to find from December through March, often in small flocks of 5-20 birds working the same stretch of rocky coast.

funFact: Purple Sandpipers are so specialized for rocky coasts that they can actually swim short distances between rocks and have been observed diving underwater to escape predators - behaviors almost unheard of in other sandpipers!
confusionNotes: The dark coloration and rocky habitat make Purple Sandpipers fairly distinctive, but they might be confused with Surfbirds (extremely rare in New England) or dark-plumaged Dunlin. Remember: if it's on rocks with orange legs and dark overall, it's almost certainly a Purple Sandpiper - other sandpipers stick to sand and mud.
compareHints: Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference. While Dunlin can appear quite dark, they have curved bills and prefer mudflats, and Sanderlings are much paler and stick to sandy beaches. The Purple Sandpiper's combination of dark coloration, orange legs, and rock-climbing behavior makes it unmistakable among New England's sandpiper family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
